questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given is a concentrated solution of a weak electrolyte $A_xB_y$ of concentration 'c' and dissociation constant 'K'. The degree of dissociation is given by :
questions.solution:
The dissociation reaction of the weak electrolyte $A_xB_y$ is:

$A_xB_y \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}$

Initial concentrations:
$c \quad 0 \quad 0$

Equilibrium concentrations:
$c(1-\alpha) \quad cx\alpha \quad cy\alpha$

The dissociation constant $K$ is given by:

$K = \dfrac{[A^{y+}]^x [B^{x-}]^y}{[A_xB_y]}$

$K = \dfrac{(cx\alpha)^x (cy\alpha)^y}{c(1-\alpha)}$

$K = \dfrac{c^{x+y} x^x y^y \alpha^{x+y}}{c(1-\alpha)}$

$K = \dfrac{c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y \alpha^{x+y}}{1-\alpha}$

For a weak electrolyte, the degree of dissociation $\alpha$ is very small, so $1-\alpha \approx 1$.

$K = c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y \alpha^{x+y}$

Solving for $\alpha$:

$\alpha^{x+y} = \dfrac{K}{c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y}$

$\alpha = \left(\dfrac{K}{c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{x+y}}$

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{K}{c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $M_3 A_2$ is a sparingly soluble salt of molar mass $y$ g mol$^{-1}$ and solubility $x$ g L$^{-1}$. The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion ($A^{3-}$) to the solubility product of the salt is
questions.solution:
The molar solubility $S$ of the salt is given by $S = \dfrac{x}{y}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

The dissociation of the sparingly soluble salt $M_3A_2$ is:

$M_3A_2 \rightleftharpoons 3M^{2+} + 2A^{3-}$

The molar concentration of the anion $A^{3-}$ is:

$[A^{3-}] = 2S$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ of the salt is:

$K_{sp} = [M^{2+}]^3 [A^{3-}]^2 = (3S)^3 (2S)^2 = 27S^3 \times 4S^2 = 108S^5$

The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion to the solubility product is:

$\dfrac{[A^{3-}]}{K_{sp}} = \dfrac{2S}{108S^5} = \dfrac{1}{54S^4}$

Substituting $S = \dfrac{x}{y}$ into the expression, we get:

$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{1}{54 \left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^4} = \dfrac{1}{54} \cdot \dfrac{y^4}{x^4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{54} \cdot \dfrac{y^4}{x^4}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Arrange the following resultant mixtures in increasing order of their pH values
A. $10$ mL $0.2$ M Ca(OH)_2$ + $25$ mL $0.1$ M HCl \\ B. $10$ mL $0.01$ M H_2$SO_4$ + $10$ mL $0.01$ M Ca(OH)_2$
C. $10$ mL $0.1$ M H_2$SO_4$ + $10$ mL $0.1$ M KOH
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For mixture A:
Millimoles of OH$^{-}$ = $10 \times 0.2 \times 2 = 4$
Millimoles of H$^{+}$ = $25 \times 0.1 \times 1 = 2.5$
Remaining OH$^{-}$ = $4 - 2.5 = 1.5$ mmol
The solution is basic, so pH $\gt 7$.

For mixture B:
Millimoles of H$^{+}$ = $10 \times 0.01 \times 2 = 0.2$
Millimoles of OH$^{-}$ = $10 \times 0.01 \times 2 = 0.2$
The solution is completely neutralized, so pH $= 7$.

For mixture C:
Millimoles of H$^{+}$ = $10 \times 0.1 \times 2 = 2$
Millimoles of OH$^{-}$ = $10 \times 0.1 \times 1 = 1$
Remaining H$^{+}$ = $2 - 1 = 1$ mmol
The solution is acidic, so pH $\lt 7$.

Therefore, the increasing order of pH values is C < B < A.

Answer: $C \lt B \lt A$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $20$ mL of a solution of acetic acid required $28.4$ mL of $0.1$ M NaOH for its neutralization. A solution (X) was prepared by mixing $20$ mL of the above acetic acid and $14.2$ mL of $0.1$ M NaOH solution. What is the pH of the solution (X)? ($pK_a$ value of acetic acid is $4.75$).
questions.solution:
For complete neutralization of $20$ mL of acetic acid, the millimoles of NaOH required is:

$28.4 \times 0.1 = 2.84$ mmol

Thus, $20$ mL of the acetic acid solution contains $2.84$ mmol of $CH_3COOH$.

For the preparation of solution (X), the millimoles of NaOH added is:

$14.2 \times 0.1 = 1.42$ mmol

The reaction between acetic acid and sodium hydroxide is:

$CH_3COOH + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3COONa + H_2O$

Millimoles of $CH_3COOH$ remaining after the reaction = $2.84 - 1.42 = 1.42$ mmol

Millimoles of $CH_3COONa$ formed = $1.42$ mmol

Since the solution contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, it forms an acidic buffer. Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

$pH = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right)$

Substituting the values:

$pH = 4.75 + \log \left( \dfrac{1.42}{1.42} \right)$

$pH = 4.75 + \log(1)$

$pH = 4.75$

Answer: $4.75$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The pH of a solution obtained by mixing $5$ mL of $0.1$ M $NH_4OH$ solution with $250$ mL of $0.1$ M $NH_4Cl$ solution is _____ $\times 10^{-2}$. (Nearest integer)
Given: $pK_b(NH_4OH) = 4.74$
$\log 2 = 0.30$
$\log 3 = 0.48$
$\log 5 = 0.70$
questions.solution:
The given mixture forms a basic buffer solution.

Millimoles of base $NH_4OH = 5 \times 0.1 = 0.5$ mmol

Millimoles of salt $NH_4Cl = 250 \times 0.1 = 25$ mmol

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:

$pOH = pK_b + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]} \right)$

$pOH = 4.74 + \log \left( \dfrac{25}{0.5} \right)$

$pOH = 4.74 + \log (50)$

We know that $\log (50) = \log (5 \times 10) = \log 5 + \log 10 = 0.70 + 1 = 1.70$

$pOH = 4.74 + 1.70 = 6.44$

The pH of the solution is given by:

$pH = 14 - pOH$

$pH = 14 - 6.44 = 7.56$

$pH = 756 \times 10^{-2}$

Answer: $756$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The first and second ionization constants of a weak dibasic acid $H_2 A$ are $8.1 \times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-13}$ respectively. $0.1$ mol of $H_2 A$ was dissolved in $1$ L of $0.1$ M HCl solution. The concentration of $HA^-$ in the resultant solution is:
questions.solution:
Given:
Weak dibasic acid $H_2A$ with $K_{a1} = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}$ and $K_{a2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13}$
Initial concentration: $[H_2A]_0 = 0.1\text{ M}$
The solution also contains $0.1\text{ M HCl}$, which dissociates completely to give $[H^+]_0 = 0.1\text{ M}$.

The main source of $HA^-$ is the first dissociation:
$H_2A \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HA^-$

Let $x$ be the amount of $H_2A$ that dissociates. Then at equilibrium:
$[H_2A] = 0.1 - x$
$[H^+] = 0.1 + x$
$[HA^-] = x$

Applying the equilibrium expression:
$K_{a1} = \dfrac{[H^+][HA^-]}{[H_2A]}$

$8.1 \times 10^{-8} = \dfrac{(0.1 + x)(x)}{0.1 - x}$

Since $K_{a1}$ is very small and the common $H^+$ ion from HCl suppresses dissociation, $x \ll 0.1$. Hence:
$0.1 - x \approx 0.1$ and $0.1 + x \approx 0.1$

$8.1 \times 10^{-8} \approx \dfrac{(0.1)(x)}{0.1} = x$

Therefore:
$[HA^-] = x = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$

The second dissociation ($K_{a2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13}$) is negligible compared to the first, so the $HA^-$ consumed in that step is insignificant.

Hence, the correct option is $(3)\ 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
At $25°C$, $20.0$ mL of $0.2$ M weak monoprotic acid HX is titrated against $0.2$ M NaOH. The pH of the solution (a) at the start of the titration (when NaOH has not been added) and (b) when $10$ mL of NaOH is added respectively, are:
Given: $K_a = 5 \times 10^{-4}$, $pK_a = 3.3$, $\alpha \lt \lt 1$
(a)(b)
questions.solution:
For part (a), at the start of the titration, the solution contains only the weak acid HX.

The concentration of HX is $C = 0.2$ M.

Using the formula for the hydrogen ion concentration of a weak acid with $\alpha \ll 1$:

$[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times C} = \sqrt{5 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.2} = \sqrt{10^{-4}} = 10^{-2}$ M

$pH = -\log(10^{-2}) = 2.0$

For part (b), when $10$ mL of $0.2$ M NaOH is added to $20$ mL of $0.2$ M HX:

Initial millimoles of HX $= 20 \times 0.2 = 4$ mmol

Millimoles of NaOH added $= 10 \times 0.2 = 2$ mmol

The added NaOH neutralizes half of the HX to form NaX, creating an acidic buffer.

Millimoles of HX remaining $= 4 - 2 = 2$ mmol

Millimoles of NaX formed $= 2$ mmol

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

$pH = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right)$

Since the millimoles of salt and acid are equal, $\log(1) = 0$.

$pH = pK_a = 3.3$

Answer: $2.0 \quad 3.3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product constants of $Ag_2CrO_4$ and $AgBr$ are $32x$ and $4y$ respectively at $298$ K. The value of $\left(\dfrac{\text{molarity of } Ag_2CrO_4}{\text{molarity of } AgBr}\right)$ can be expressed as :
questions.solution:
Let the solubility of $Ag_2CrO_4$ be $S_1$.

For $Ag_2CrO_4 \rightleftharpoons 2Ag^+ + CrO_4^{2-}$

$K_{sp} = (2S_1)^2(S_1) = 4S_1^3$

$4S_1^3 = 32x \Rightarrow S_1^3 = 8x \Rightarrow S_1 = 2\sqrt[3]{x}$

Let the solubility of $AgBr$ be $S_2$.

For $AgBr \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Br^-$

$K_{sp} = S_2^2$

$S_2^2 = 4y \Rightarrow S_2 = 2\sqrt{y}$

The ratio of their molarities is:

$\dfrac{S_1}{S_2} = \dfrac{2\sqrt[3]{x}}{2\sqrt{y}} = \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{x}}{\sqrt{y}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{x}}{\sqrt{y}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the dissociation equilibrium of the following weak acid
$\mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq})+\mathrm{A}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})$
If the pKa of the acid is 4, then the pH of 10 mMHA solution is $\_\_\_\_$.(Nearest integer)
[Given: The degree of dissociation can be neglected with respect to unity]
questions.solution:
For the weak acid dissociation $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$ with pKa = 4
We have Ka = 10⁻⁴.
For a 10 mM (0.01 M) solution where the degree of dissociation is negligible with respect to unity, the concentration of HA remains approximately 0.01 M.
The equilibrium expression gives
$Ka = \frac{[H^+]^2}{[HA]}$
Substituting: $10^{-4} = \frac{[H^+]^2}{0.01}$, which yields $[H^+]^2 = 10^{-6}$, so $[H^+] = 10^{-3}$ M.
Therefore, pH = $-\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider two Group IV metal ions $\mathrm{X}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$. A solution containing $0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{X}^{2+}$ and $0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Y}^{2+}$ is saturated with $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$. The pH at which the metal sulphide YS will form as a precipitate is $\_\_\_\_$. (Nearest integer)
(Given: $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{XS})=1 \times 10^{-22}$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{YS})=4 \times 10^{-16}$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, $\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}\right]=0.1 \mathrm{M}$ in solution, $\mathrm{K}_{a 1} \times \mathrm{K}_{a 2}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}\right)=1.0 \times 10^{-21}, \log 2=0.30$, $\log 3=0.48, \log 5=0.70$)
questions.solution:
$XS(s) \rightleftharpoons X^{+2}(aq.) + S^{2-}(aq.)$
For precipitation of $XS(s)$
$[X^{+2}][S^{2-}] \geq K_{sp}(XS)$
$[S^{2-}] \geq \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-22}}{0.01} = 10^{-20}$
$YS(s) \rightleftharpoons Y^{+2}(aq) + S^{2-}(aq)$
For precipitation of $YS(s)$
$[Y^{+2}][S^{2-}] \geq K_{sp}(YS)$
$[S^{2-}] \geq \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-2}} = 4 \times 10^{-14}$
Now, $H_2S(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2H^+(aq) + S^{2-}(aq)$
$\dfrac{[S^{2-}][H^+]^2}{H_2S} = K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2} = 1 \times 10^{-21}$
$[S^{2-}] = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-21} \times [H_2S]}{[H^+]^2} \geq 4 \times 10^{-14}$
$[H^+]^2 \leq \dfrac{1}{4} \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{-1}$
$[H^+] \leq \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-4} \Rightarrow pH \geq 4.3$
Nearest integer pH = 4.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The first and second ionization constants of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{X}$ are $2.5 \times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-13}$ respectively. The concentration of $\mathrm{X}^{2-}$ in $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{X}$ solution is $\_\_\_\_\times 10^{-15} \mathrm{M}$. (Nearest Integer)
questions.solution:
For a weak diprotic acid $H_2X$, the ionization steps are:
$H_2X \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HX^-$ with $K_{a1} = 2.5 \times 10^{-8}$
$HX^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + X^{2-}$ with $K_{a2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13}$
Since $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2}$, the concentration of $H^+$ is primarily determined by the first ionization.
$[H^+] \approx \sqrt{K_{a1} \cdot C} = \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.1} = \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-9}} = 5 \times 10^{-5} M$
Also, from the first ionization, $[HX^-] \approx [H^+] = 5 \times 10^{-5} M$
For the second ionization:
$K_{a2} = \frac{[H^+][X^{2-}]}{[HX^-]}$
Substituting the values: $1.0 \times 10^{-13} = \frac{(5 \times 10^{-5})[X^{2-}]}{5 \times 10^{-5}}$
Thus, $[X^{2-}] = K_{a2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13} M$
To express this in the form $x \times 10^{-15} M$:
$1.0 \times 10^{-13} = 100 \times 10^{-15} M$
The value is 100.

[Assume $\alpha$ is negligible with respect to 1 ]
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \\ & \mathrm{t}=0 \quad 1 \mathrm{~mole} \\ & \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{eq}} \quad 1-\alpha \quad \alpha \quad \frac{\alpha}{2} \\ & \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{T}}=1+\frac{\alpha}{2} \simeq 1(\alpha \ll 1) \\ & \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2} \cdot \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{O}_2}^{1 / 2}}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}}}=\frac{(\alpha \cdot \mathrm{P})\left(\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathrm{P}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(1-\alpha) \mathrm{P}} \\ & 8 \times 10^{-3}=\frac{\alpha^{3 / 2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \alpha^{3 / 2}=8 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-3} \\ & \alpha^3=128 \times 10^{-6} \\ & \alpha=\sqrt[3]{128} \times 10^{-2} \\ & =5.03 \times 10^{-2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Which one of the following arrangements represents the correct order of the proton affinity of the given species :
questions.solution:
The species with the greatest proton affinity will be the strongest base, and its conjugate acid will be the weakest acid. The weakest acid will have the smallest value of $\mathrm{K}_a$. Since $\mathrm{HI}$ is a stronger acid than $\mathrm{HF}$ which is a stronger acid than $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{S}$, a partial order of proton affinity is 
$\mathrm{I}^{-} \lt  \mathrm{F}^{-} \lt  \mathrm{HS}^{-}$
Since $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is a very weak acid, $\mathrm{NH}_2^{-}$must be a very strong base. Therefore the correct order of proton affinity is
$\mathrm{I}^{-} \lt  \mathrm{F}^{-} \lt  \mathrm{HS}^{-} \lt  \mathrm{NH}_2^{-}$
